title: Relationship between the parts of a complex number with its conjugate
text:
Edit (2024-07-13): $\mathrm{arg}(z) = \frac{1}{i}\ln\sqrt{\frac{z}{\bar z}}$ is true only for $z>0$, so it is irrelevant. It is not the case for all $z \in \mathbb{C}-\{0\}$. So, the relationship asked is valid only for the functions of the real part and absolute value.
Edit (2024-07-14): Substitution of previous definitions for the imaginary part and the argument of a complex number $z$ to another that is valid and preserves the relationship asked in the question. Also, formatting.

The parts of a complex number $z$ can be represented alongside its conjugate $\bar z$ as variables with the real part as $\mathrm{Re}(z) = \frac{z+\bar z}{2}$, imaginary part as $\mathrm{Im}(z) = \frac{z-\bar z}{2i}$, absolute value as $\mathrm{abs}(z) = \sqrt{z \bar z}$, and argument as $\mathrm{arg}(z) = \frac{1}{i}\ln\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{z\bar z}}\right)$ for $z\neq 0$.
But there is a relationship between the real part and the absolute value, the same way that there is a relationship between the imaginary part and the argument of the complex number z. Rewriting to make some operations explicit:
$$ \mathrm{Re}(z) = \left(z+ \bar z \right)2^{-1} $$
$$ \mathrm{abs}(z) = \left(z\cdot \bar z \right)^{ 2^{-1} } $$
$$ \mathrm{Im}(z) = (z +(z +\bar{z}){2^{-1}}({-1}))i^{-1} $$
$$\mathrm{arg}(z) = \ln(z \cdot(z \cdot\bar{z})^{{2^{-1}}({-1})})i^{-1} $$
From the real part to the absolute value, addition becomes multiplication and multiplication by $2^{-1}$ becomes exponentiation by $2^{-1}$. From the imaginary part to the argument, again, addition becomes multiplication, and multiplications by $(-1)$ and $2^{-1}$ become exponentiations (not considering the natural logarithm).
Something similar happens when we represent complex numbers in rectangular and polar form, if a unique symbol for the complex constant $e^i$ is used, which will be represented as $\varrho$:
$$z = a+ ib = r\cdot\varrho^{\theta}.$$
Is there a connection that explains this?

Proof. Assume ring $R$ has maximal ideal $0$. Then for any $u\in R$, it follows $(u)=R$. Noting that $(u)=R\{u\}R$, we deduce there exist $a,b\in R$ such that $aub=1$. title: The first integral cohomology of a smooth manifold is torsion free?
text:
Suppose we have a good cover $U_{\alpha}$ of M. Then the Cech cohomology with respect to this cover is isomorphic to the singular cohomology. So just consider the problem by Cech cohomology.
We have a homomorphism $i:H^{1}(U_{\alpha},\mathbb{Z})\to H^{1}(U_{\alpha},\mathbb{Q})$ for the constant $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{Q}$ sheaves. For a cocycle $u_{\alpha\beta}\in H^{1}(M,\mathbb{Z})$, if $i(u_{\alpha\beta})=0$, this means that $u_{\alpha\beta}=\delta f$ for some $f_{\alpha}\in C^0(U_{\alpha},\mathbb{Q})$. Then if we choose an open set $U_{\alpha_{0}}$, and define $g_{\alpha}=f_{\alpha}-f_{\alpha_{0}}$, it is easy to see that $g\in C^{0}(U_{\alpha},\mathbb{Z})$ because of good cover and $\delta g=u$. Thus $i$ is injective and consequently $H^{1}(U_{\alpha},\mathbb{Z})$ must be torsion free.
Here is some details for the easy to see part. Since we are working with good covers, $g_{\alpha}$'s are constant on $U_{\alpha}$'s because $f_{\alpha}$'s are. For any $U_{\alpha}$ intersects $U_{\alpha_{0}}$, we have $g_{\alpha}=g_{\alpha_{0}}-u_{\alpha\alpha_{0}}$ hence it is an integer. Then by connectedness of $M$, all $g_{\alpha}$'s are integers.

title: Linearization of ODE flows on manifolds about arbitrary solutions
text:
On Euclidean space, for an ODE
$$\dot x_t = F(x_t)$$
there is a natural linearization about $x_t$ given by
$$\dot y_t = y_t \cdot \nabla F(x_t).$$
On a manifold $M$, if we have a vector field $V$, we get the ODE flow
$$\dot x_t = V(x_t).$$
Intuitively, it seems like one should be able to describe the linearization of this ODE flow in a way that is independent of Riemannian metric, but we see in the Euclidean case that we have to differentiate the vector field $V$, which usually requires a connection. What is the correct intrinsic way to linearize an ODE flow given by a vector field on an arbitrary smooth manifold? Does it require a metric, and if so is the solution metric dependent?
This question is similar to this post, which concerns differentials of the flow map, which is of course very related to linearization of the ODE. The post did not receive a full answer though, and I take a different perspective here.

title: How to expand a symmetric triple sum?
text:
I'll start with a double sum example:
$$\sum_{n,l}f_{n}f_{l}\frac{\partial^{2}g}{\partial x_{n}\partial x_{l}} = \sum_{n}f_{n}^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}g}{\partial x_{n}^{2}}+2\sum_{n<l}f_{n}f_{l}\frac{\partial^{2}g}{\partial x_{n}\partial x_{l}},\qquad n,l \in [1,N]$$
This is not a simplification, but it greatly reduces the number of arithmetic operations needed to evaluate the result. The right hand side is intuitive as we can imagine all the terms arranged on a square grid, then the first sum is the diagonal terms and the second sum is upper (or lower) triangle.
We can also check the number of terms on the left $|N^2|$ and on the right $|N+2(N^2-N)/2=N^2|$, which is correct.
Now for a similar triple sum seems to expand like this:
$$\sum_{m,n,l}f_{m} f_{n}f_{l}\frac{\partial^{3} g}{\partial x_{m}\partial x_{n}\partial x_{l}} = \sum_{n}f_{n}^{3}\frac{\partial^{3}g}{\partial x_{n}^{3}}+3\sum_{n\neq l}f_{n}^{2}f_{l}\frac{\partial^{3}g}{\partial x_{n}^{2}\partial x_{l}}+\sum_{m\neq n\neq l}f_{m}f_{n}f_{l}\frac{\partial^{3}g}{\partial x_{m}\partial x_{n}\partial x_{l}}$$
But it's not very helpful, since there's hardly any gain in the number of operations reduced. So what am I missing?
My combinatorics is bad, it's my weakest area of math.

title: Can power of three have a lot of leading 9
text:
I came up with this problem, but was unable to either prove or disprove the statement.
Let $dig(n)$ be the number of digits in the decimal representation of $n$. Is it true that $dig(3^n+2^n)=dig(3^n)$ when $n \geq 3$ is a natural number?
Of course, $\frac{dig(3^n)}{dig(2^n)}=\frac{ln(3)}{ln(2)}$ approximately, which is around $1.5$. So in order that to happen $3^n$ should have a lot leading nines, namely around $1-\frac{ln(2)}{ln(3)}$ percent of all digits, which is around $37$ percent. One possible approach is to consider log base 10 of $3^n$, but it didn't really lead me to anything vital. To be precize, in order for $3^n$ to start with $k$ nines, $nlog_{10} 3$ mod $1$ should be in the range $[log_{10} (10^k-1)$ mod $1,1)$. The length of it is $l=log_{10}(\frac{10^k}{10^k-1})$, then $\frac{1}{l}=log_{1+\frac{1}{10^k-1}}(10)$, which is approximately $ln(10)10^k$. Then by Diophantine's theorem there exists an $n \leq ln(10)10^k$ such that $3^n$ starts with $k$ nines. But in this estimation $k$ is asymptoticly $log_{10}(n)$, however we need a constant multiplied by $n$. 
Unfortunately, that was the only idea that popped into my mind.

title: Must a sequentially discrete subspace of a LOTS itself be a LOTS?
text:
By LOTS I mean linearly ordered topological spaces.
Suppose that $X$ is a LOTS, and $Y$ is a sequentially discrete subspace of $Y$, meaning that any sequence contained in $Y$ that has a limit in $Y$ is eventually constant. Must the subspace topology of $Y$ induced by some order on $Y$? Note that such order may not coincide with the order inherited from $X$.
As a trivial example, if $Y$ is a discrete subspace of $X$, then such order exists because every discrete space is a LOTS. On the other hand, I have constructed an example of sequentially discrete LOTS that is not discrete in this MSE question.
Note that $Y$ is anticompact, meaning that every compact subset $Y$ is finite: Suppose that $Z$ is a compact subset of $Y$ (in the subspace topology), then the subspace topology of $Z$ coincides with its topology induced by the order on $X$ (a coarser Hausdorff topology and a finer compact topology must coincide); in particuler, $Z$ is a compact LOTS, so it is sequentially compact (as a countably compact LOTS is: Every sequence has a monotone subsequence and it converges), then sequential discreteness of $Z$ implies finiteness.
The problem is that I do not know many examples of a subspace of LOTS that is not itself a LOTS. An such example is the disjoint union of $\mathbb{R}$ and a singleton. You can see here for a proof that it is not a LOTS, but such a proof uses the fact that $\mathbb{R}$ is connected. Here we have instead a totally disconnected space: any nontrivial closed inteval in a connected LOTS must have cardinality $\ge\mathfrak{c}$ as any nontrivial connected $T_4$ space does.
Thank you in advance for any help.

title: Are all continuous functions that send conics to conics in $\mathbb{R}^2$ a generalized linear fractional transform?
text:
Motivation:
Consider an arbitrary conic section in $\mathbb{R}^2$ given by
$$ Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0 $$
Now consider the map $$\phi: \mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2, \phi_{\begin{pmatrix} a & b & c \\ d & e & f \\ g & h & i \end{pmatrix} }(x,y) = \left( \frac{ax + by + c}{dx+ey+f}, \frac{gx+hy+i}{dx+ey+f} \right)  $$
This map sends a conic section to a conic section. This is easy enough to verify with algebra by observing that if for some (x,y):
$$ Ax^2 + Bxy + Cy^2 + Dx + Ey + F = 0 $$
Then there exists an $x'$ and $y'$ s.t. (if $\phi$ is invertible)
$$ A \phi(x')^2 + B\phi(x')\phi(y') + C\phi(y')^2 + D\phi(x') + E\phi(y') + F  = 0$$
And therefore
$$ A  \left( \frac{ax' + by' + c}{dx'+ey'+f} \right)^2 + B  \left( \frac{ax' + by' + c}{dx'+ey'+f} \right) \left(  \frac{gx'+hy'+i}{dx'+ey'+f} \right) + C \left(  \frac{gx'+hy'+i}{dx'+ey'+f} \right)^2 + D \left( \frac{ax' + by' + c}{dx'+ey'+f} \right) + E  \left(  \frac{gx'+hy'+i}{dx'+ey'+f} \right)  + F  =  0 $$
But by multiplying out all the denominators and grouping like powers of $(x')^n(y')^m$ we can clearly see that  $(x',y')$ itself lies on some conic section.
So then (it feels clear to me that) we can conclude $\phi$ sends a conic section to a section.
The question:
Now is this set of $\phi$ the ONLY continuous functions $\mathbb{R}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^2$ that send conics to conics?
Or do there exist some more exotic functions with this property?
It does seem this family of functions is well known as the set of homographies which I found out about via this question.

title: Absolutely vs Non-Absolutely Convergent Infinite Product
text:
Consider the following standard infinite product:
$$
 \prod_{n=1}^{+\infty} \left( 1 + \frac{(-1)^n}{2n-1}z \right)
$$
This product is not absolutely convergent because:
$$
 \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} \left| \frac{(-1)^n}{2n-1}z \right| \text{ has the same character as } \sum_{n=1}^{+\infty} \frac{1}{n}
$$
however, by writing it as:
$$
 \prod_{n=1}^{+\infty} \left( 1 - \frac{z}{4n+1} \right) \left( 1 + \frac{z}{4n-1} \right)
$$
it becomes absolutely convergent.
The key step in writing it out this way is the following:
$$
\prod_{n=1}^{+\infty} \left( 1 + \frac{(-1)^n}{2n-1}z \right) = \lim_{N \to +\infty} \prod_{n=1}^{2N} \left( 1 + \frac{(-1)^n}{2n-1}z \right)
$$
where I can consider $2N$ only, because the sequence associated to the product converges to 1.
I would like to know wether this analysis is correct or not, and if so, does that mean that "collecting product terms in different ways may change the character of convergence"? (I guess something similar happens for series if we collect terms of a conditionally convergent alternating sign series in a way such that we end up with a positive sign series which is absolutely convergent).

title: Let $f$ be a continuous function mapping the unit interval to the unit interval such that $\int_{0}^{x}f = \int_{x}^{1}f$. Prove that $f=0$.
text:
Let $f$ be a continuous function mapping the unit interval to the unit interval such that $\int_{0}^{x}f = \int_{x}^{1}f$. Prove that $f=0$.
I´ve tried doing a proof by contradiction. Suppose that $f\neq0$ so that there exists some $x_{0} \in (0,1)$ such that $0<f(x_{0})\leq 1$. Since $f$ is continuous, there exists a neighbourhood of $x_{0}$ where $f>0$. Thus we can pick $\delta\geq r >0$ such that $f(x)>0$ for all $x\in(x_{0}-\delta, x_{0}+\delta)$. Now note that
$$
0= \int_{0}^{0}f = \int_{0}^{1}f.
$$
Hence,
$$
0 = \int_{0}^{1}f = \int_{0}^{x_{0}-\delta}f + \int_{x_{0}-\delta}^{x_{0}+\delta}f + \int_{x_{0}+\delta}^{1}f.
$$
Since the integral preserves the order, we have $0<\int_{x_{0}-\delta}^{x_{0}+\delta}f\leq 1$. Similarly $0\leq \int_{0}^{x_{0}-\delta}f \leq 1,\ 0\leq \int_{x_{0}+\delta}^{1} f \leq 1$. So the right hand side of the equality is stricttly greater than $0$, which implies that $0>0$, a contradiction. I´m not sure if this is correct because the fact that $f(x)\leq 1$ is not strictly neccesary in my proof. I´ve also thought about using $F(x) =\int_{0}^{x} f$ for $x\in [0, 1]$ and trrying to prove that $F' = 0$. I could use Rolle´s theorem to find some $c\in(0,1)$ where $F'(c) = 0$, but that is just some point not the whole interval. Another thing I´ve noticed is that in that case $F$ is Lipschtz with Lipschitz constant 1, since
$$
|F(x)-F(y)| = F'(c)|x-y|\leq |x-y|
$$
for some $c\in(x,y)$ where $x$ and $y$ are arbitrary. But I don´t know right now if this could be useful in this case.

title: Neural network that learns ODE's 'refuses to learn' initial conditions
text:
I have implemented a simple network that for now i'm just trying to teach the ODE:
$$\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} = x$$
Using the simple code below:
import tensorflow as tf
from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense
from tensorflow.keras.optimizers import Nadam

import numpy as np

#Simple NN
model = Sequential([
    Dense(5, input_dim=1, activation='relu'),
    Dense(5, activation='relu'),
    Dense(1)
])

#Define parameters
n_epochs = 500

#And time over which we train
timestep = 0.05
time = np.arange(0,5,timestep)

opt = Nadam(learning_rate=0.02)

#Custom training loop using PINN loss.
for e in range(n_epochs):
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:
        x = model(time)
        dx = [(x[i+1]-x[i])/timestep for i in range(len(x)-1)]
        loss = sum((x[1:]-dx)**2)
        print(loss)
    grad = tape.gradient(loss, model.trainable_variables)
    opt.apply_gradients(zip(grad,model.trainable_variables))

title: Relation between mean and $\beta$ parameter of discrete Boltzmann distribution with degeneracies
text:
I am trying to compute the mean $\bar{E}$ of a Boltzmann distribution
$$ 
p(\pmb{x}) = \frac{1}{Z} e^{-\beta E(\pmb{x})},
$$
knowing that there is a total of $N$ microstates $\pmb{x}$ and $[\alpha N]$ energy levels, and that each energy level has degeneracy ${N}\choose{E}$, $E \in \{1, 2, \ldots, [\alpha N]\}$, for some $\alpha$ is fixed in $[0, 1]$.
In the case $\alpha=1$, I was able to compute $\bar{E}$ analytically from the partition function:
$$
Z = \sum_{\pmb{x}} e^{-\beta E(\pmb{x})} = \sum_{E=0}^{N} {{N}\choose{E}} e^{-\beta E} = (1 + e^{-\beta})^N
$$
and so
$$
\bar{E} = - \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta}\log Z = \frac{N}{1 + e^\beta}.
$$
I am not able to compute $\bar{E}$ for a generic $\alpha \in [0, 1]$, though. In particular, it seems that there is no analytic expression for the truncated sum $\sum_{E=0}^{[\alpha N]} {{N}\choose{E}} e^{-\beta E}$ (see https://mathoverflow.net/questions/93744/estimating-a-partial-sum-of-weighted-binomial-coefficients?rq=1).
My final goal though is not to compute $Z$, but to study $\bar{E}$ as a function of $\beta$, for any fixed $\alpha$ in the unit interval. Ideally, I would like to have a way to compute $\beta$ given $\bar{E}$. Any ideas on how I could go about this? Approximations of $\beta$ given $\bar{E}$ would also be very useful. Thanks!

text:
I'm struggling a bit how to apply a standard solution to the heat equation to my own practical problem. I have some intuition, but do not know whether this intuition is justified. I don't understand the math well enough. My two questions are:

Is it correct to "scale and add" the partial solutions as I describe below? (if not, how can I solve it instead?)
What is the proper mathematical terminology to describe the solution? ("additivity"?)

My problem:
Suppose I put a hot sphere in a colder bath, and I want to know the temperature profile in the sphere. If the sphere starts out at homogeneous temperature, this problem has a standard solution. In non-dimensional form and for $\tau > 0.2$ we may approximate:
$$
 \frac{T(R) - T_{A}}{T_i - T_{A}} = \Theta_A(R,\tau) = A_1 e^{-\lambda_1^2\tau}\frac{\sin(\lambda_1 R)}{\lambda_1 R}
$$
Where $T_{A}$ temperature of the liquid in the batch,  $T_i$ the initial temperature of the sphere, $\Theta_A$ the dimensionless temperature, $R$ a positional coordinate that scales from 0 in the center to 1 at the surface of the sphere, $\tau$ the Fourier number a.k.a. dimensionless time, $\lambda_1$ the first eigenvalue of the heat equation and $A_1$ a constant that only depends on $\lambda_1$. For $\tau <0.2$ I need to add the second, third, etc. eigenvalue. I leave those out here for the sake of simplicity.
Now I take that sphere at some time $\tau_1 = \infty$, and place it in bath B, which has a temperature $T_{B} < T_{A}$. At $\tau_B = \infty$ I have $T(R) = T_A$ as initial condition, so I can re-use the previous solution with slight modification:
$$
 \frac{T(R) - T_{B}}{T_A - T_{B}} = \Theta_B(R,\tau) = A_1 e^{-\lambda_1^2\tau}\frac{\sin(\lambda_1 R)}{\lambda_1 R}
$$
So far, so good.
Now I change the situation. I don't wait until infinity, but I move that sphere to bath B at some time $\tau_B \ll \infty$. I now no longer have a homogeneous initial condition for the sphere that goes into bath B.
My intuition tells me that I can add both solutions, by re-mapping them to $\Theta_{overall} = \frac{T(R) - T_{B}}{T_i - T_{B}}$:
$$
\Theta_A(T_A) = 0 \Leftrightarrow \Theta_{overall}(T_A) = \frac{T_A - T_{B}}{T_i - T_{B}}
$$
$$\Rightarrow \Theta_{overall}(R,\tau) = \Theta_A(R,\tau)(1-\Theta_{overall}(T_A)) + \Theta_B(R,(\tau - \tau_B))\Theta_{overall}(T_A)$$
when $\tau - \tau_B > 0.2$.
It is easy for me to show that this works out if $\tau_B = 0$, and that the re-scaling works fine for the case where the bath B is entered with a sphere at homogeneous $T_A$. I am, however, at a loss when I want to show that I am justified to do this for $0 < \tau_B \ll \infty$.

title: How to obtain the first law of BH mechanics from the Smarr formula
text:
In general relativity coupled to electromagnetism in $d$ dimensions, the Smarr formula relates the thermodynamical variables present in a rotating, electrically charged black hole. More specifically, it may be expressed as
\begin{equation}
M=\frac{d-2}{d-3} \left(TS+\Omega_\mathcal{H}^n J_n\right)+\left(\Phi_\mathcal{H}-\Phi_\infty\right)Q
\end{equation}
where $M$ denotes the mass of the black hole spacetime, $T$ its temperature, $S$ the entropy, $\Omega_\mathcal{H}^n$ and $J_n$ the angular velocities and momenta respectively, $\Phi_{\mathcal{H},\infty}$ the electrostatic potential at the horizon and infinity respectively and $Q$ the electric charge.
The first law of BH mechanics relates the variation of the thermodynamical variables with each other. In the same setting, it reads:
\begin{equation}
\delta M=T\delta S+\Omega_\mathcal{H}^n\delta J_n +(\Phi_\mathcal{H}-\Phi_\infty)\delta Q
\end{equation}
It is often stated that the Smarr formula is the "integrated" version of the first law, but both of them are usually obtained via different methods.

I was wondering how one could directly obtain the first law from the Smarr formula by performing directly a variation of the Smarr formula. Using the chain rule, one encounters terms like $\delta \Omega_\mathcal{H}^n J_n$ and $\delta T S$, and I do not know of any way of expressing $\delta T$ as a linear combination of $\delta M, \delta J, \delta  Q$ and $\delta S$.
I can obtain expressions like $T=\frac{\partial M}{\partial S}$, but I do not see how this helps.
One way of solving this issue is if I was able to compute $\frac{\partial T}{\partial M}, \frac{\partial T}{\partial J}$ and so on, since therefore, $\delta T=\frac{\partial T}{\partial M}\delta M +\frac{\partial T}{\partial J}\delta J+\dots$
Furthermore, I cannot use Euler's homogeneity theorem to obtain the previous derivatives, as the temperature, angular velocity etc. are not extensive quantities.
I guess this question may be rephrased in purely thermodynamical terms, maybe as how to obtain the variation of the chemical potentials associated to the charges in terms of the variation of the charges.

title: How are objects inside a black hole affected by the gravity of objects outside the black hole?
text:
There are many Q&As about whether something inside a black hole can escape the event horizon if another massive object gets close enough to pull it out. I realize the answer (I think universally agreed?) is no because the geometry inside the horizon simply allows for no paths leading out of it.
A follow up to that question which I haven't seen addressed is whether gravity from an object outside the black hole - say a binary twin that is either also a black hole or just shy of it - affects the spacetime geometry inside the black hole, and thus the objects inside, in any way.
For example, suppose you're freefalling inside an SMBH and another massive object (maybe a black hole, maybe not, but I think it shouldn't matter) is in a stable orbit and not on a path to merge with the one you're in. Do you feel the pull of the external object and how does that impact your inevitable journey to the singularity? Is there any configuration that could pull you back toward the horizon (even if you can't cross it?) Will it simply slow you down but never cause you to reverse your path (a form of time dilation almost)?
A Penrose diagram or animation illustrating how the internal geometry of the black hole changes as another supermassive object nears it would - if available - likely be extremely helpful. I think I can imagine one but am definitely not qualified to try to create it and wouldn't know if it was accurate.

title: Viscous stress, and closed dynamic equations for density and velocity fields of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process?
text:
Context
I am trying to write simple derivation of hydrodynamic definition of viscous stress $\partial^{2}_{x}v$ based on OU-process which is
\begin{align}
\dot{x} &= v \\
\dot{v} &= -\gamma v + \xi
\end{align}
Question
Does this process have $\partial^{2}_{x}v$ in the momentum equation? i.e does $\partial_{t}v$ have a term $\partial^{2}_{x}v$ in it?
What is the simplest way to generalize OU to derive viscous stress ? i.e what is most simple stochastic equation giving rise to viscous stress ?
How to derive Newton's law of viscous stress ?

title: Can you tell who is moving through time?
text:
In relativity, there is no way to tell if you are moving through space. So, if you were inside of a box, there would be no way for you to tell if you were moving or not. However, can you know who is moving through time? Could you just turn on a flashlight while you are inside of a box and count the light travel time, in meters, going by?
And if you CAN tell who is moving through time, does this mean there is actually a preferred frame of reference?
Does the rule that there are no preferred frames of reference ONLY APPLY to movement through space, or does this rule ALSO APPLY to movement through time?
We know photons do not travel through time. So, could this be used as a reference frame?

title: How does the Fermi level of graphene change if it is placed in a biased pn junction or in a plate capacitor?
text:
I ran into a problem on which I can't really find any solutions in literature. I am looking at a Graphene sheet that is sandwiched in a biased pn junction (current flows orthogonal to the Graphene layer). Graphene seems to be an almost transparent tunelling barrier, so the depletion region width still changes under bias even with the graphene layer inbetween.
What I don't really get is why the graphene's fermi level changes? Is the carrier concentration in the 2D sheet actually changing? And can I treat the reverse bias case as if the Graphene would sit in the middle of a capacitor? If so how would I go about calculating the Fermi level change as a function of the applied voltage?
Thanks a bunch in advance!

title: Why does this RLC behavior differ from what equations predict?
text:
In order to better understand RLC behavior under current sources, I constructed the simple circuit below and attempted to analyze it.  However, my equations do not agree with simulation results.
The equations are simple, and use standard calculus, yet they don't seem to produce correct results.

My analysis is in some ways consistent with simulation but in some ways gets very different results.  Is my analysis correct? If so, why does it not agree with simulation?
I've already asked about this on an electronics site.  While they confirmed that simulation does not agree with the equations, no one was able to spot any error in them or suggest more correct ones.  So I decided I needed to ask here.
Analysis shows: $$ V_{out} = I_{src} \omega^2 LCR_{load}$$ since
$$
I_{src} = I_0 e^{j \omega t} \\
V_{L1} = V_1 - L \frac{dI_{src}}{dt} \\
= V_1 -jI_{src} \omega L$$ and $$
I_{load} = C \frac{dV_{L1}}{dt} \\
= \omega^2 L C I_{src}$$
so $$V_{out} = I_{load}R_{load} \\
= I_{src} \omega^2 LCR_{load}.
$$
This suggests that $V_{out}$ is linear in $L, C, R$ and quadratic in $f$ and should be in phase with $I_{src}$. However, when I simulate it, I find that similar relationships, but not exact, and that $V_{out}$ hits a limit at a few MHz after which increasing $f$ has no effect.  Why?

title: Chain rule with functional derivative?
text:
I posted the same question on math exchange but no answer yet, so I post it also here:
"I'd like to make the functional derivative of the functional $S[\phi(x)]$ with respect to the Fourier transform $\widetilde{\phi}(p)$ such that
$$\phi(x)=\int\frac{d^{d}p}{(2\pi)^{d/2}}e^{ip\cdot x}\widetilde{\phi}(p)$$
Can I use the following chain rule
$$\frac{\delta S}{\delta\widetilde{\phi}(p)}[\phi]=∫{d^{d}x}\frac{\delta\phi(x)}{\delta{\widetilde{\phi}}(p)}\frac{\delta S}{\delta\phi(x)}[\phi]=∫ \frac{d^{d}x}{(2\pi)^{d/2}}e^{ip\cdot x}\frac{\delta S}{\delta\phi(x)}[\phi]$$
or not?"
